goal: Working on speaking up in meetings; has social anxiety about it.

priorChatTurns.text: Your last three reps all held under 5 fillers — the mechanics are landing. Next step is saying the hard sentence without softening it.
I know what I'm supposed to do but in the actual meeting I just freeze.

emotionalSignal: fatigue and quiet discouragement — this is a vulnerable admission, not a request for a drill; he's telling you the gap between practice and the real room is heavy

goal.whyNow: wants to stop going silent when it counts
goal.visionOfSuccess: say the one thing he came in wanting to say, once, out loud

recentReps.note: held composure through a simulated interruption

memoryState.subjectivePattern: Repeatedly reports freezing in real meetings despite clean practice reps — a confidence/transfer gap, treated as a hypothesis, not a diagnosis.

liveCoachingFrame.emotionalRegister: sit with it briefly, don't rush to a drill

expectedCoachMove: Meet the emotion first — acknowledge that it genuinely isn't easy and that the freeze is real, without therapy-speak or minimising. Then, lightly, anchor to evidence that the capacity is already there (held composure through an interruption this week) so the encouragement is earned, not hollow. At most a small, low-pressure next step — or just presence. Do NOT lead with a drill or a metric.
badAnswerExample: I understand your frustration. Here are some tips: 1) prepare talking points, 2) practice more, 3) think about your audience. The key is to keep practicing and be more confident. You've got this!
excellentAnswerExample: No, it's not. Knowing the move and doing it when the room's watching are two different things — the freeze is the real work, not a failure of it. Worth remembering though: this week you held it together through an interruption. That version of you exists. You don't have to be fearless in there — just say one sentence before the fear votes. One.
